Target
TAR-get
noun
A diminutive of the Old French targe, “a light shield,” from a Frankish root; hence a small shield or buckler carried on the arm. The modern sense — the mark one shoots at — arose only later, when shields were set up to be shot at in practice.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In the KJV a target is a shield. The word names a piece of defensive armour — a small shield or buckler borne before the body — and the modern reader must reverse his instinct to read it rightly. We hear target and think of the thing aimed at: the mark, the bullseye, the object of attack. The KJV means the thing held before you: the guard, the cover, the plate that takes the blow. The word’s history explains the reversal — old shields were set up as marks for archery practice, and in time the name of the shield passed to the mark it was used for, until the defence became the object of assault. Scripture shows the target in three lights. It is a giant’s armour: Goliath “had greaves of brass upon his legs, and a target of brass between his shoulders” (1Sa 17:6), and all that brass availed him nothing against a boy with a sling and the name of the LORD of hosts. It is a king’s treasure: “king Solomon made two hundred targets of beaten gold: six hundred shekels of gold went to one target” (1Ki 10:16) — shields too precious to fight with, hung in the house of the forest of Lebanon for glory, and carried off by Shishak within a generation. And it is a godly king’s honest war-gear: Asa had three hundred thousand men of Judah that bare targets and spears (2Ch 14:8), and with them he cried to the LORD and was heard. Above all three stands Paul’s word: “Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked” (Eph 6:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

A shield or buckler borne on the arm — the thing held before you, not the thing aimed at.

TARGET, a shield or buckler; a piece of defensive armour borne before the body.

A diminutive of Old French targe, “a light shield.”

The later sense — a mark to shoot at — came from shields set up for archery practice.

Goliath wore a target of brass between his shoulders (1Sa 17:6).

Solomon made two hundred targets of beaten gold for the house of the forest (1Ki 10:16).

Key Scripture

1Sa 17:6 — "And he had greaves of brass upon his legs, and a target of brass between his shoulders."

1Ki 10:16 — "And king Solomon made two hundred targets of beaten gold: six hundred shekels of gold went to one target."

2Ch 14:8 — "And Asa had an army of men that bare targets and spears, out of Judah three hundred thousand; and out of Benjamin, that bare shields and drew bows, two hundred and fourscore thousand: all these were mighty men of valour."

Eph 6:16 — "Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked."

Modern Corruption

A word that has turned inside out: the KJV’s target is the shield you hold, while ours is the mark you shoot at — defence become object of attack.

expand to see more

Here is a genuine reversal, and it is worth naming plainly because it trips every modern reader of 1Sa 17:6. A target in the Authorized Version is a shield. Our target is a bullseye. The one is what covers you; the other is what is shot at. The drift happened honestly enough — men set old shields on posts and shot at them for practice, and the name of the armour slid over to the mark — but the result is that a word which once meant protection now means prey. A reader who does not know it will picture Goliath with a bullseye between his shoulders rather than a plate of brass, and will miss the point: the giant was armoured head to heel and still fell, because no target of brass turns the stone that God sends.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond that honest drift of language. The principle to recover is which target a man trusts. Goliath had one of brass and died in it. Solomon made two hundred of beaten gold, six hundred shekels apiece — too costly to carry into any battle, hung on the wall for show — and Shishak king of Egypt took every one of them away, and Rehoboam replaced them with brass. That is the fate of every golden target: the glory a man hangs on his wall is carried off by the next invader. Asa’s three hundred thousand bore honest targets and spears, and when the Ethiopian host came out against him he cried, “LORD, it is nothing with thee to help,” and the LORD smote them. The armour is not nothing; but the arm is everything. Above all, take the shield of faith.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means a shield or buckler borne before the body — not the mark shot at.

expand to see more

Target — a diminutive of Old French targe, “a light shield.”

In the KJV it always means a shield, never a mark to aim at.

The modern sense arose from shields set up as marks for archery.

Goliath’s target was of brass; Solomon’s were of beaten gold.

The believer’s target is the shield of faith, quenching fiery darts (Eph 6:16).

Usage

"A target of brass between his shoulders: the KJV’s target is armour, not a bullseye."

"Solomon’s golden targets never turned a blow — and Shishak carried every one of them away."

"Asa’s men bore targets and spears, and their king bore something better: a cry to the LORD."
